scenes.tts: The first film traced which changes can reach offspring. If an allele is dominant, must most individuals carry it? Watch a few blue cards move through this group.
scenes.caption: The first film traced which changes can reach offspring. If an allele is dominant, must most individuals carry it? Watch a few blue cards move through this group.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: genes and alleles blue; environment green; acquired body changes gold; routes to offspring teal; stopped routes red; other structures grey. Hook first. A large transparent population bowl fills most of the frame. Many grey allele cards and a few blue allele cards circulate slowly. Grey outlines of individuals surround the bowl. A question mark grows above the few blue cards. Mark the whole display schematic.
scenes.narration: The first film traced which changes can reach offspring. If an allele is dominant, must most individuals carry it? Watch a few blue cards move through this group.

scenes.visual: Brief title card after the hook: Dominant Is Not Popular. Keep the moving schematic bowl and its few blue cards visible behind the title.

scenes.tts: An allele is a version of a gene. In this simple model, an individual receives one copy from each parent. The pair is its genotype. The trait that appears is its phenotype. Dominant and recessive describe how the pair of allele copies affects that phenotype.
scenes.caption: An allele is a version of a gene. In this simple model, an individual receives one copy from each parent. The pair is its genotype. The trait that appears is its phenotype. Dominant and recessive describe how the pair of allele copies affects that phenotype.
scenes.visual: Keep the bowl at left and enlarge one individual at right. A teal route carries one card from each of two parent outlines into two large genotype slots. The paired cards settle. Below them, an empty phenotype window waits. Labels appear only when used: allele on one card, genotype under the pair, phenotype under the window.
scenes.narration: An allele is a version of a gene. In this simple model, an individual receives one copy from each parent. The pair is its genotype. The trait that appears is its phenotype. Dominant and recessive describe how the pair of allele copies affects that phenotype.

scenes.tts: A dominant allele shows its trait even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive. So a dominant allele can mask a recessive allele in one individual. Neither word means stronger, healthier, or better.
scenes.caption: A dominant allele shows its trait even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive. So a dominant allele can mask a recessive allele in one individual. Neither word means stronger, healthier, or better.
scenes.visual: Place one blue dominant card and one grey recessive card in the genotype slots. The phenotype window lights blue and reads shows. Replace the blue card with a grey card; only then does the window turn grey. Keep a separate strength gauge neutral and crossed out when stronger, healthier, and better are spoken. The bowl continues moving at left.
scenes.narration: A dominant allele shows its trait even when only one copy is present. A recessive allele shows its trait only when both copies are recessive. So a dominant allele can mask a recessive allele in one individual. Neither word means stronger, healthier, or better.

scenes.tts: Only a few blue allele cards are in this group. When one blue card enters a genotype pair, will its trait show? Decide before the window changes.
scenes.caption: Only a few blue allele cards are in this group. When one blue card enters a genotype pair, will its trait show? Decide before the window changes.
scenes.visual: Return almost all cards to the schematic bowl, leaving only a few blue among many grey. One blue card travels slowly toward a genotype slot holding one grey card. Freeze it just outside the slot. Keep the phenotype window neutral. Show the question Will the trait show? above the pair.
scenes.narration: Only a few blue allele cards are in this group. When one blue card enters a genotype pair, will its trait show? Decide before the window changes.

scenes.visual: Thinking pause. Keep the blue card hovering outside the genotype slot and the phenotype window neutral. All cards in the bowl drift slowly. Do not reveal the answer.

scenes.tts: The blue card enters, and the trait shows. That is dominance inside this individual. Yet the population bowl still contains very few blue cards. The rule for showing changed the phenotype window. It did not make the allele common in the group.
scenes.caption: The blue card enters, and the trait shows. That is dominance inside this individual. Yet the population bowl still contains very few blue cards. The rule for showing changed the phenotype window. It did not make the allele common in the group.
scenes.visual: Slide the blue card into the open slot. Light the phenotype window blue. At the same time, keep the bowl's blue cards few and unchanged. Draw two independent displays: shows in this individual beneath the pair, and common in this group beneath the bowl. The first rises; the second stays low. Label both displays schematic.
scenes.narration: The blue card enters, and the trait shows. That is dominance inside this individual. Yet the population bowl still contains very few blue cards. The rule for showing changed the phenotype window. It did not make the allele common in the group.

scenes.tts: Now move more blue cards into the bowl without changing the showing rule. The group display rises. Move them out, and it falls. The individual display still follows the allele pair. Frequency belongs to the group. Dominance belongs to the relationship between alleles.
scenes.caption: Now move more blue cards into the bowl without changing the showing rule. The group display rises. Move them out, and it falls. The individual display still follows the allele pair. Frequency belongs to the group. Dominance belongs to the relationship between alleles.
scenes.visual: Keep the genotype pair fixed. Pour additional blue cards into the schematic bowl; raise only the common-in-group display. Remove most blue cards; lower only that display. Then swap the genotype pair between blue-grey and grey-grey; change only the shows-in-individual display. Use smooth transformations, never a list of labels.
scenes.narration: Now move more blue cards into the bowl without changing the showing rule. The group display rises. Move them out, and it falls. The individual display still follows the allele pair. Frequency belongs to the group. Dominance belongs to the relationship between alleles.

scenes.tts: A dominant trait may be common or rare. A recessive trait may also be common or rare. These are separate questions. One asks what an allele does beside another allele. The other asks how many copies exist across a whole group.
scenes.caption: A dominant trait may be common or rare. A recessive trait may also be common or rare. These are separate questions. One asks what an allele does beside another allele. The other asks how many copies exist across a whole group.
scenes.visual: Transform the two displays into a large two-axis map marked showing rule and group frequency. Move one blue-grey genotype marker between dominant and recessive examples while the bowl marker moves independently between common and rare. Mark every position schematic. Do not show real trait names, counts, or any values from the lesson's data table.
scenes.narration: A dominant trait may be common or rare. A recessive trait may also be common or rare. These are separate questions. One asks what an allele does beside another allele. The other asks how many copies exist across a whole group.

scenes.tts: The everyday word dominant can sound like winning. Genetics uses it more narrowly. It describes how a phenotype appears when different alleles share a genotype. It does not say one allele will spread, replace another, or become common. Population frequency is a separate pattern to measure.
scenes.caption: The everyday word dominant can sound like winning. Genetics uses it more narrowly. It describes how a phenotype appears when different alleles share a genotype. It does not say one allele will spread, replace another, or become common. Population frequency is a separate pattern to measure.
scenes.visual: Keep the schematic pair and bowl side by side. A gold trophy labelled winning approaches the word dominant, then stops at a red barrier and fades. Blue arrows labelled spread and replace also stop before the population bowl without changing any cards. The genotype pair continues to control only its phenotype window. The bowl remains a separate measured pattern.
scenes.narration: The everyday word dominant can sound like winning. Genetics uses it more narrowly. It describes how a phenotype appears when different alleles share a genotype. It does not say one allele will spread, replace another, or become common. Population frequency is a separate pattern to measure.

scenes.tts: To test a claim about commonness, count traits or alleles in a defined group. To test dominance, follow which phenotypes appear in offspring, as Mendel did with peas. One kind of evidence cannot replace the other. Later courses add inheritance patterns beyond simple dominance.
scenes.caption: To test a claim about commonness, count traits or alleles in a defined group. To test dominance, follow which phenotypes appear in offspring, as Mendel did with peas. One kind of evidence cannot replace the other. Later courses add inheritance patterns beyond simple dominance.
scenes.visual: Carry the two displays forward. Under group frequency, animate grey person icons entering a counter with no numbers shown. Under showing rule, animate parent allele pairs sending teal card paths into offspring pairs and phenotype windows. Keep both evidence streams separate. Add a small forward arrow labelled more patterns later, without naming new patterns.
scenes.narration: To test a claim about commonness, count traits or alleles in a defined group. To test dominance, follow which phenotypes appear in offspring, as Mendel did with peas. One kind of evidence cannot replace the other. Later courses add inheritance patterns beyond simple dominance.

scenes.tts: So when you hear dominant, look inside one genotype pair. Ask whether a copy shows beside a different allele. When you hear common, look across the whole group. Ask how often the allele, or its trait, occurs. Never use one answer for both questions.
scenes.caption: So when you hear dominant, look inside one genotype pair. Ask whether a copy shows beside a different allele. When you hear common, look across the whole group. Ask how often the allele, or its trait, occurs. Never use one answer for both questions.
scenes.visual: Zoom in on the genotype pair when dominant is spoken, then zoom out to the full schematic bowl, labelled whole group, when common is spoken. Place a teal divider between the displays. The pair's phenotype window and the bowl's frequency display continue moving independently. Fade all labels except dominant, common, and the divider before the end card.
scenes.narration: So when you hear dominant, look inside one genotype pair. Ask whether a copy shows beside a different allele. When you hear common, look across the whole group. Ask how often the allele, or its trait, occurs. Never use one answer for both questions.

scenes.visual: End card. Show one line only: 'Dominant tells how an allele shows, not how common it is.'
